Google Ads audit

A Google Ads audit from someone with no incentive to flatter you

Most free PPC audits are sales documents: they find enough problems to justify a proposal and stop. This is a paid, fixed-scope account audit that ends with a prioritised list of fixes you own, whether or not you ever hire me again.

What a PPC audit usually uncovers

Different companies, different industries, and the same short list of problems. These are the ones that show up in most Google Ads audits I run, roughly in order of how much money they waste.

Conversions counted more than once

The same lead fires as a form submission, a thank-you pageview and a phone call. Your reported cost per lead is fiction, and Smart Bidding has been optimising towards the fiction for months.

Search terms nobody has read

In neglected accounts, a double-digit share of budget routinely goes to queries that will never convert: job seekers, students, competitors' brand names, the wrong country.

Structure built for the tool

Campaigns organised by match type or by whoever built them, instead of by margin, service line and geography, which is what you actually make decisions on.

Automation on defaults

Broad match with Smart Bidding and no negatives. Performance Max with no brand exclusion, quietly buying demand you already had. Auto-applied recommendations switched on.

Budget where the margin is not

The cheapest service to sell receives the most budget because it produces the most conversions, while the profitable one is capped. Correct by the platform's logic, wrong by yours.

Landing pages that leak

Ads promising one thing, pages offering another; forms that fail on mobile; call buttons that are not tracked. The account can be perfect and still lose here.

What the audit covers

  1. Measurement first. Every conversion action, its source, its counting method and its attribution setting. GA4 and Tag Manager configuration. Consent mode. Whether the numbers in Google Ads can be reconciled with the CRM. If this layer is wrong, nothing below it can be trusted, so it is checked before anything else.
  2. Search terms and negatives. Twelve months of search terms against what you sell, with an estimate of the spend that produced nothing. Negative lists proposed by campaign and shared.
  3. Structure and settings. Campaign and ad group organisation against the business, location and language settings, network settings, ad schedules, device adjustments, and the change history that explains how the account got here.
  4. Bidding and budgets. Strategy per campaign against its data volume, target settings, budget-limited campaigns that should not be and unlimited ones that should, portfolio strategies and their side effects.
  5. Ads, assets and Performance Max. Ad strength as a symptom rather than a goal, asset coverage, brand exclusions, asset group logic, feed quality for Shopping.
  6. Landing pages and conversion path. Message match, speed on mobile, form and call tracking, what happens after the lead arrives.

The deliverable is a written document with findings ranked by financial impact, each with the fix, who should do it and how to confirm it worked, plus a short call to walk through it. Accounts on Microsoft Advertising or Meta can be added to the same audit; see PPC management and Meta Ads.

Why the audit is paid

A free audit has to be paid for somehow, and it is paid for by the retainer it is designed to sell. That shapes what it finds. A paid audit can say "the account is in decent shape, fix these three things and keep your current setup", and I have written exactly that more than once. Many clients take the audit, implement it themselves or with their existing team, and never hire me for management. That is a good outcome, not a failed sale.

The price is fixed and quoted from the form, based on account size and how many platforms are in scope. It is the same price whether or not you go on to work with me, and it is credited against the first month if you do.

Questions people ask before hiring

How much does a Google Ads audit cost?

A fixed price quoted from the form, based on monthly spend, number of campaigns and platforms in scope. It is credited against the first month of management if you hire me afterwards. See pricing for the models.

How long does a PPC audit take?

Five to seven working days from receiving access, for a typical single-platform account. Larger or multi-platform accounts take longer and the quote says so up front.

What access do you need?

Read-only access to Google Ads, GA4 and Google Tag Manager, and ideally a CRM export or a conversation with whoever handles the leads. I do not change anything during an audit.

Do I have to hire you afterwards?

No. The report is yours to implement however you like. A meaningful share of audit clients implement it in-house and that is fine.

Can you audit Meta Ads, Microsoft Advertising or LinkedIn Ads too?

Yes. Each platform adds scope and a bit of time, and it is worth doing them together because the tracking layer is shared.

Will you tell me if my agency is doing a good job?

Yes, in writing. I have no retainer to win by criticising them, and a fair audit that confirms the agency is competent is still useful: it tells you where the remaining gains are.
